B1_RazAlon_damage_first_passage.outcome: NO CONTACT. The SR damage model is Markov in X; the paper's death event is already a first passage (of a level by a non-circular variable, not of arc on a circle). The core's history variable adds nothing once X is known (AUC near 0.5 within an X band), while X itself predicts death (AUC well above 0.5). The regime question the paper leaves open (ballistic vs quasi-steady tracking) is about the SR drift, not about path geometry.

B3_NguyenZacks_event_triggers.outcome: REDUCES, with the CRR-specific part WRONG for this purpose. A third trigger type (accumulated change since the last boundary, as opposed to an error peak) does mark slow-drift boundaries the error trigger misses, so the idea is live for the paper's residual variance. But the core's version of it, accumulated ARC, is dominated by noise path length on any real carrier and fires continuously (false alarms above), whereas the standard displacement-since-last-boundary (chord, CUSUM-type) trigger catches the same boundaries with few false alarms. What survives is the rival, not the core. A prospective test on OpenNeuro ds005551 would add a displacement trigger to the paper's model; the core contributes the question, not the detector.

B4_Blattner_excess_cost_identifiability.outcome: REPHRASE with one transferable constraint. The paper's 'excess cost along the trajectory' and 'baseline-relative endpoint displacement' are the core's surplus and chord in another vocabulary (independent formulation, not a CRR influence). The core's identifiability result transfers as a caution: excess cost cannot carry information beyond (path cost, displacement); a model that uses all three is rank-deficient. Whether hidden regenerative state is a path quantity at all is the paper's own open prediction and nothing in the core decides it.
